section_summary: This section of the file (pages 74–111) contains documents compiled and transmitted by U.S. Consul Richard F. Boyce from Yokohama regarding American citizens of Japanese descent (Nisei) residing in Japan. It comprises the concluding pages and reference appendices of a printed survey handbook advising Nisei students on social adjustment, educational entry requirements, and nationality laws, followed by three specific enclosures. These enclosures include a radio broadcast transcript on employment opportunities by Tosuke Yamazaki, an essay translation and student writings compiled by S. Natori advocating the traditional Japanese spirit over Western materialism, and the complete Autumn 1939 issue of the quarterly periodical 'Pan-Pacific Youth' published by the Japan-America Young People's Federation.

subfiles.about: Concluding section and reference appendices of an informational handbook and survey for American-born Japanese residing and studying in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This concluding portion of a survey and guidebook addresses the vocational, educational, and cultural adjustment problems confronting Nisei in Japan, encouraging self-reliance, practical ambition, and pride in their Japanese heritage while warning against institutions that exploit foreign students. Detailed appendices set forth Japanese Department of Education regulations for student certification, essential U.S. statutory provisions on nationality, expatriation, and military liabilities, and comprehensive directories of Nisei youth organizations and secondary and higher educational institutions admitting Nisei in Japan.
subfiles.title: [Survey and Guidebook for Nisei Residing and Studying in Japan]

subfiles.about: Radio broadcast transcript discussing vocational realities and employment prospects for Nisei in Japan and East Asia.
subfiles.summary: Tosuke Yamazaki's radio address says Japan is not a land of boundless opportunity for English-speaking Nisei: rising costs, tough competition, falling wages, Japanese and technical skills required, and mainland Asia demands pioneering fortitude.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 2: Nisei Opportunities in Japan (KAIGAI 'Let's Tune In' Hour)

subfiles.about: Translation of an ideological essay and student compositions examining Nisei identity, the Japanese Spirit, and the China Incident.
subfiles.summary: Lecturer S. Natori contrasts Western and American individualism, hedonism, and materialism with the Japanese Spirit (Yamato Damashii), defined by selfless loyalty, ancestral reverence, and devotion to the Emperor and the Imperial Way. He justifies Japan's military campaign in China as a holy mission to liberate Asian peoples from Western colonial subjugation and Soviet communism, exhorting Americanized Nisei to study the Japanese language and awaken to their ancestral virtues to serve as cultural bridges. The document also reproduces three reflective essays written by Waseda International Institute students Yoshio Inoue, Tomomi Naito, and Isamu Kumai on their evolving perspectives regarding the China Incident, heritage education, and balancing individualism with communal duty.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 3: The Ideals of the Second-Generation Japanese and the Japanese Spirit

subfiles.about: Autumn 1939 issue of 'Pan-Pacific Youth', an English-language quarterly magazine published by and for Nisei in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Transmitted as Enclosure No. 4 to a consular report by Richard F. Boyce, this issue of the quarterly organ of the Japan-America Young People's Federation features editorials, essays, social news, and organizational reports. Highlights include an editorial by Ken Murayama urging community support, Amy Murayama's travelogue of Shanghai and Nanking, contrasting male and female views on marriage choices between Nisei and native Japanese, and the federation's 1939 election results. It further includes a humorous prophecy imagining council members' lives in 1954, an account of a student tour through Kyushu, a philosophical piece supporting Frank Buchman's Moral Re-Armament movement, an exposé of delinquency and vice in Pacific Coast communities by 'A. E. H.', and an inside description of the Overseas Department of the Broadcasting Corporation of Japan.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 4: Pan-Pacific Youth, Vol. I, No. 2 (Autumn 1939)
